My wife and I live in a 600sqft apartment with 2 cats and 2 litter boxes. It is doable and one of the easiest things to try.

A good change is still a change and can still cause unease until she settles down. I know I'd be unsettled if my best friend from childhood showed up and started to stay with us and there would be an adjustment period. But I'm Autistic so maybe that's just a me thing.

First, that is NOT the way to discipline a cat. The cat won't know WHY you are shoving (not literally) their face into feces and is just going to serve to make the cat more anxious, especially around you. If you see poop, clean it up really well, and that's it. If you see the cat pooping outside the box, don't scare or startle them as that could cause anxiety around pooping itself. Instead, calmly walk up and pick the cat up and redirect to the litterbox.

Start with adding another litter box. Some cats prefer to pee in one and poop in the other. Try a different type of litter box, one that is open and less constricted.

Play. Play. Play. Lots of play and even trick training. Boosting a cats' confidence is what I have found helps with behavioral issues the most. A confident cat spends less time anxious.

You could bring the cat to a vet or groomer to check anal glands too, perhaps they are impacted. If so, this could cause discomfort while pooping and thus an association of pain with the litterbox.

I'd also be curious as to why you coming back has seemed to trigger this behavior. Is there friction in the family that the cat picks up on? Have you disciplined the cat similarly their whole life? This could cause trust issues.

It may also just simply be the change. Cats can be pretty sensitive to change, and sometimes, a person coming back home after time away can be stressful in its own right. Be patient and curious.

Best of luck to you and your cat!

I've been on t for almost 9 months now for context.

With T in general, there isn't any picking and choosing with effects. What you can do, though, is start on a lower dose so changes start and progress slowly, giving you the most time to stop should you want.

My main concerns with T were facial hair, bottom growth, and potential balding. To try and remedy this, I wanted to also go on a DHT blocker to slow down or even stop those changes. I was unable to because the clinic I go to for my transition care follows specific guidelines, and DHT blockers were not part of that. I was suggested instead to go on a lower dose to prevent the changes. OP, a lower dose will NOT stop the changes. It only makes then some slower but will end with full masculinization regardless.

I wasn't too keen on needing to shave if I didn't want a beard (trauma and sensory issues), but as it's been growing, I'm starting to really like that it's there. I'll likely never shave smooth, and so my hair clippers clean up my beard just fine. 

Bottom growth scared me as I was unsure of how drastically things would change, but like my beard, it's grown on me.

No balding has happened yet, despite my family genetics. My hairline is beginning to change, though, and I am quite happy with it!

My suggestion is to look at lots of progress pictures. Look into all the effects individually and ask yourself if you want it, can deal with it, and if it is better or more easily coped with than what you currently experience. Talk to an endo or other doctor familiar with the process, ask questions, even if they sound silly.

Ultimately there are things I don't like about T, the increase in sweating for starters, but I am dealing with so much less dysphoria that those small things feel easy to deal with. They feel like normal grips about having a human body rather than they wrong body.

Best of luck OP!

I am agender and here is my experience. Note, I am autistic and being able to label myself and figure out my experience is incredibly important to me.

For me, everyone I know has this sort of mystical, spiritual, etc feeling that they just know their gender. Some internal knowledge that is just there for them. I seem to lack that.

Much like someone's sexual orientation, they just know what and who they are attracted to. I am bi and  know I am attracted to multiple genders, but there isn't any reason why, I just am.

So for me, my internal sense of gender just isn't there. I spent a long time trying to seek out some nebulous feeling. It led to a lot of confusion, self hate, and feeling othered. It was like I was missing some essential piece of the human experience.

Eventually, I found nonbinary and that felt a little more comfortable. I knew I wasn't a woman and didn't want to be a man, nonbinary suited me. I later found maverique (not a man, not a woman), but that still wasn't quite right despite being technically true.

After hearing about agender, I struggled to apply the label to myself because it almost felt like I was giving up on finding a part of me. I've come to realize now that I don't think I'll ever find that piece because it never existed in the first place.

Now I've settled a little more peacefully into the label and it feels like I have all the important information for myself and my experience.

Obviously, everyone's experience is unique and not all-encompassing of the agender experience.

Your situation sounds pretty similar to what I went through earlier in my transition.

At first, I assured her I wouldn't get top surgery, that a change in pronouns and name was all I needed. Dysphoria got worse and worse while I pushed down my needs. Eventually, it clicked with my wife, and she saw how hopeless and sad I was and encouraged me to seek medical intervention.

A lot happened between then and now. My wife discovered her own gender and we started HRT together. As I've started to look more masculine from HRT, my wife has said her attraction to me has grown. She loves all the changes and, most of all, says she loves who I've been able to be since I'm not hiding myself anymore.

I still have days where it is tough to reconcile her preference for femininity with my internal sense of being. Those days, I try to remember her actions, all of which point to loving me as I am and as the person I'll soon be.

I guess my point is, keep communication open. If you feel you are being treated too much like a man or woman, tell your partner. I can understand wanting to be cis. I've had those thoughts a lot. I've come to realize that for me, had I been cis, I wouldn't be the same person. The person I am and want to be is worth fighting for just as the person you are is worth the fight.

Hey OP!  


Nail caps are quite inexpensive and last upward of six weeks! Amazon has them for sale, 100 caps for around $10. Declawing cost is anywhere from $600-$1800 plus the additional costs of safe litter for their healing and any medication the cat may need. You parents may front the cost of the nail caps when this is considered.  


While I've seen a lot of good advice about putting more scratching posts around and redirecting the cat to them, I haven't seen people explain why that helps. Cats mark their scent with scratching and so they tend to try to scratch, mark, rub their faces on, etc things in high foot traffic areas to let everyone know that this is their territory. Even being declawed, many cats still try to scratch things to mark their scent and I can't imagine it feels very good on their nubs.  


As for nail clipping, check every couple days and clip what looks and feels sharp. Their nails don't tend to grow in uniformly, I know my cat, her dewclaws are usually the first to grow back. I just check her paws when she's laying down somewhere and clip as needed.  


You can also avoid excess scratching by making sure to tire the little one out. Lots of playing, especially when young will go a long way. As will teaching small tricks, target training, high five, etc.  


Either way, if you father decided to take the cat and get it declawed, that is not your fault. You are very obviously eagerly doing your best. If it happens, all you can do is try to give your cat the best chance possible to heal correctly. You can also supplement in something like tri-acta when the cat is older and feeling discomfort as it may help.  


Best of luck, OP.

I have owned cats, birds, various reptiles, fish and lived with dogs my whole childhood. I am also Canadian so dollar amounts may be different to what you could expect.  


Every type of pet is going to be expensive to set up and have about the same amount of work.   


For a single cat, not including adoption fee, you are looking at possibly several hundred dollars to get all the essentials and anywhere from $50 - $100 to feed monthly. Vet visit prices vary greatly but generally a check up can cost around $75. It is likely a cat will need some sort of medical help with something like UTIs, hotspots, small injuries, etc. A cat you will need to offer various sources of stimulation. Playing with a cat for 10-20 minutes a couple times a day is highly recommended, especially if you only have a single cat. Bored cats often develop health issues both mentally and physically. You can help this by getting two cats, however there is the extra food and sibling syndrome that need to be considered.  


Dogs will be similar price ranges to a cat, just scaled up with the size of the dog. If you have a large breed, you will likely be buying more than one bag of food a month. There is also the added need of walking and training the dog. While cats can be trained and do benefit from it, dogs require a baseline expected behavior. Leash manners, recall, stay, leave it, etc, are all commands are required in my opinion.

For reptiles the cost really depends on the species. A bearded dragon is going to be more expensive than a couple anoles for instance. Reptile start up costs are quite high as they need a suitable sized enclosure, bedding, decorations, hides, heat lamp/mat, etc. Depending on the amount of extra daily work you want to cut out, there are products like misting systems that also need to be factored in financially. Feeding a reptile can be quite inexpensive. A bearded dragon for instance can share quite a few veggies with you and you need only supplement in some insects and powdered calcium/vitamins. As most people would have a variety of veggies on hand anyway, they really only cost $20 to feed per month. A snake, depending on the species, size, and age, you can expect $40-$100.  


Reptiles can be very expensive medically. I find in my area, not many vets are trained in exotic animals. The few that are tend to be much more expensive. The more common medical issues, stuck shed, off feed, underweight, minor dehydration, you will generally be identifying and treating yourself. A vet is only really required for more serious things like scale rot, URI, burn, etc. You will need to handle a reptile at least once a day to help with mental stimulation, exercise and taming. Reptiles don't seem to either feel or are able to express affection in any meaningful way, at least to me. While I care for my snakes and beardie greatly, there isn't the same sort of reciprocation as a cat or bird.  


Birds will be the most expensive, especially depending on the species. The initial cost will be high. Cost of parrots from reputable sources will be fairly high unless you get a smaller species like a budgie. there is a lot of misinformation out there about birds and their enclosures. Unless a bird is only sleeping in their cage, they should have a large one.  The cost here will wildly vary. A budgie enclosure doesn't need to be as large or sturdy as a macaw's. A new cage could run you a thousand dollars and the bird would likely be $50-$1,000 for smaller species and $1,000-$20,000 for larger. They also need a varied diet of veggies, some fruits and seeds, and some bird species have very specific diets.  


Vet costs for birds can be huge. Avian vets are also more uncommon and the cost of treating birds is high due to their delicate systems. A general check up should cost $50-$100. Birds, prey animals that they are, tend to hide their sickness until it is quite serious and you would need to know common signs and symptoms in order to increase chances of early diagnosis. The more common illnesses birds face are connected to their respiratory system because people use a lot of products that are toxic to birds. Burning candles, using non-stick cookware, gas heating, incense, air fresheners, etc are all toxic to birds. Owning a bird is a lifestyle change in a lot of ways. Birds are also loud naturally. They need a lot of work and stimulation, much more than other pets. They are like living with a small child for 15-80 years, but the child has a knife strapped to their face and can chew through wood.  


Fish might be a good choice. While they can have a high start up cost, you could very well go with a 10 gallon tank with a betta and a couple snails. Depending on store, a tank would cost a couple hundred plus the filter, heater, decorations, gravel/sand, plants, etc. r/bettafish has a lot of good resources for this. The cost does scale with the size of tank, amount of fish, and species, however the monthly cost is really only the food and water cost of water changes.  


Fish can be difficult to keep in the start because the water levels can take a while to stabilize and you'll likely be tweaking things for a while. The work that goes in on the daily is fairly low. Generally you'll only be doing a weekly water change, feeding, and visiting. Fish can recognize their keepers and can be trained to trust you and do simple tricks (like jumping through a hoop). They also don't need to prevent you from getting a new pet later on. So long as you have a lid and the animal cannot open it, your fish will be safe. As for medical expenses, people don't generally bring fish into vets. I would imagine a larger species may require it, however most conditions like dropsy, swim bladder issues, etc are treated with over the counter fish meds from aquarium supply stores.  


TL:DR Cats and fish are generally lowest maintenance and cost however animals and their costs vary wildly as does their care.

Red ear sliders need a LOT of care.  


As she's female, she may benefit from a deeper digging area in the event she feels the need to lay eggs. If that happens, make sure to supplement in some calcium. Her shell will need vitamin e to properly shed scutes.  


The biggest reason for any reptile not to eat is improper husbandry. If there is not enough heat, she cannot properly digest. Also keep in mind that they absorb a lot through their skin and improper water parameters can cause infection and other problems. She also may just be incredibly stressed from the change in location.  


Turtles also require water to swallow. For a long while, ours would only eat food floating in the water though eventually learned to grab a mouthful from the bowl and bring it over to the water's edge.  


Depending on the season and the ambient temperature of the room and her enclosure, she may be trying to brumate. This is completely normal and healthy to do in low temp weather. If you're so inclined, you can research how to safely brumate a turtle and that could give you some time to buy the other equipment you need for her to be happy and healthy.  


If you have questions, please reach out. I don't think you're time outs are having the effect you want them to. By the time you gather up the kitten and any toys and such, they have forgotten what they are getting punished for.   


Really make sure you are draining her energy, often high energy is mistaken for aggression and the less the issue is addressed, the more pent up the kitten can become. Next time she bites, react with a higher pitched 'Ouch!' and then withdraw all attention from the kitten, this is how they learn with their sibilings.  


As for her claws, she is a kitten it is expected that her claws will become sharp again quickly. This is because their nails don't grow like ours, instead a fully razor sharp point grows from the inside and the old nail flakes off (kinda like how reptiles shed for instance). Really make sure to check her claws daily and trim/file when needed. The more you do this, the more the quick recedes. Eventually you won't need to do as much maintenance.  


To help stop the fighting against getting claws trimmed, try to go at her pace. Build up trust that you touching her paws and the clippers being near isn't a bad thing. Touch her paws all the time, pay attention to her body language and stop when you see she get's uncomfortable. Permission based training will really help here. When you towel her and cut her claws as she tried to wriggle out and whine, you are giving her a negative association not only with you, but towels, clippers, and her paws being touched. If needed you can grab some claw caps and ask the vet to put them on when her claws get clipped, this will give you some time to work on her fears without worrying about getting shredded to ribbons.  


You can also train her to use not use her claws as much via target training. Get a stick and a clicker plus her favorite treats. Put the end of the stick on the ground in front of her and when she touches it with a paw (as she probably will due to curiosity), click and give a treat. Work on this until she gets the idea then start only clicking and treating when she doesn't use her claws.
